intro: A Torah scroll is read with a silver pointer. A Qur'an is kept on a high shelf and recited in Arabic by people who speak many languages. A Sikh scripture rests under a canopy and is honored as a living Guru. Before this course studies any single religion, it asks a basic question: what makes a text sacred to a community, and how can someone from inside or outside that community read it carefully?

This unit gives you the tools. You will ask who gave or wrote a text, for whom, when and why. You will see how texts moved from memory and recitation to scrolls, codices, palm leaves and printed books, and how communities decided which books belong in their scripture. You will learn why every translation is also an interpretation, and how rabbis, church councils, Muslim scholars and gurus have guided their communities' readings.

You will also learn the rules of the academic study of religion in a public school: describe, attribute and do not rank. Chicago itself offers an example, from the World's Parliament of Religions of 1893 to the many houses of worship in the city today. By the end of the unit, you will be able to read a passage from any tradition, explain it in terms its adherents would recognize and compare two traditions fairly.
bigQuestion: How can a careful reader understand a sacred text on its own terms, and compare traditions fairly without judging them?

timeline.t: Jewish scholars in Alexandria begin translating the Hebrew scriptures into Greek, the Septuagint
According to tradition, the Pali Canon of Buddhism is first written down in Sri Lanka
The Mishnah records the Oral Torah, as Jewish tradition describes it
The Council of Nicaea produces an early form of the Nicene Creed
Athanasius of Alexandria lists the 27 books of today's New Testament
Jerome completes the Latin translation later called the Vulgate
Muslims believe the Qur'an was revealed to Muhammad over these years
The Gutenberg Bible is printed in Mainz, Germany
The King James Version of the Bible is published in English
The World's Parliament of Religions meets in Chicago
The first Dead Sea Scrolls are found in caves near Qumran
The U.S. Supreme Court rules in Abington v. Schempp on religion in public schools

words.d: writing that a community sets apart as holy, authoritative or revealed
a message that believers hold was made known by God or a divine source
the people a text was first written or spoken for
the time, place and situation in which a text was written or first heard
knowledge, stories or teachings handed down by speaking and memory rather than writing
an early form of the book, made of sheets folded and sewn along one edge
a community's official list of books it accepts as scripture
a kind of writing, such as law, story, poetry, prophecy, letter or teaching
an explanation of what a text means; every translation includes some
a way of reading in which people and events in a text stand for something else, often spiritual
Muslim scholars trained in the Qur'an, the Hadith and Islamic law
variety of beliefs and practices inside a single religious tradition

test.q: Which statement best explains what makes a text sacred?
choices: It is very old
It is written in gold ink
A community sets it apart and shapes its life by it
It is kept in a museum
test.why: Scholars define a sacred text by its relationship to a community that treats it as holy or authoritative.

test.q: In Luke 1:3-4, the author names Theophilus and explains why he writes. Which two things does the passage reveal?
choices: Genre and canon
Translation and date
Author and archaeology
Audience and purpose
test.why: Luke names his reader, Theophilus, and his purpose, that the reader may know the certainty of what he was taught.

test.q: What does the Hindu term shruti describe?
choices: The Vedas, understood as truths heard by ancient sages
The epics, understood as remembered stories
A Buddhist monastery
A Sikh prayer
test.why: Shruti means what was heard and refers to the Vedas; smriti, what was remembered, includes the epics.

test.q: Which practice is an example of oral tradition today?
choices: Printing a Bible in Mainz
A hafiz reciting the whole Qur'an from memory
Listing books in a canon
Writing a commentary
test.why: A hafiz has memorized the entire Qur'an, keeping the text through memory and recitation.

test.q: Why do Catholic and Protestant Old Testaments have different numbers of books?
choices: Protestants added Maccabees
Catholics removed the Psalms
They were translated from different languages
Catholics include books such as Tobit and Judith
test.why: Catholics and Orthodox include books such as Tobit, Judith and Maccabees, which Protestants call the Apocrypha.

test.q: Psalm 23 says, The LORD is my shepherd. Which genre is this, and how should it be read?
choices: Law, as a rule for shepherds
Letter, as an answer to a church
Poetry, reading the shepherd as an image
Prophecy, as a prediction
test.why: Psalm 23 is poetry, so the shepherd is an image of care, not a job description.

test.q: What did the Supreme Court allow in Abington School District v. Schempp (1963)?
choices: Objective study of religion as part of a secular education
Required daily Bible readings
Teachers leading prayer
Choosing one official school religion
test.why: The Court struck down devotional readings but said objective study of religion is consistent with the First Amendment.

test.q: The KJV reads Thou shalt not kill; the 1917 JPS reads Thou shalt not murder. What does this show?
choices: One Bible has a printing error
Every translation involves choices of interpretation
The verses come from different books
Hebrew has no word for killing
test.why: The Hebrew verb has no exact English match, so each translation reflects an interpretive choice.

test.q: How did the Septuagint affect the reading of Isaiah 7:14?
choices: It removed the verse
It translated almah as parthenos, usually meaning virgin
It translated the verse into Latin
It placed the verse in the Qur'an
test.why: The Greek Septuagint rendered almah as parthenos, the form Matthew quotes, shaping Christian reading of the verse.

test.q: What is peshat in Jewish interpretation?
choices: An allegorical reading
A church council
A Greek translation
The plain meaning of a verse
test.why: Peshat is the plain meaning of a verse, as in the commentary of Rashi.

test.q: How did the rabbis of the Talmud interpret eye for eye in Exodus 21:24?
choices: As payment of money equal to the injury
As a call for revenge
As an allegory about the soul
As a rule for kings only
test.why: The rabbis concluded that the verse requires monetary compensation for an injury.

test.q: Which group teaches sola scriptura, scripture alone, as the highest authority?
choices: Catholics
Sunni ulama
Protestants
Orthodox Jews
test.why: Protestant reformers such as Luther taught sola scriptura; Catholics look to the magisterium alongside scripture.

test.q: What do Sikhs believe about the Guru Granth Sahib since 1708?
choices: It is a history of India
It replaced the Vedas for Hindus
It must be read only in English
It is the eternal Guru
test.why: Sikhs believe that Guru Gobind Singh ended the line of human Gurus and the scripture became the eternal Guru.

test.q: Which sentence follows the rules describe, attribute and do not rank?
choices: Buddhists teach that all things are impermanent.
Buddhism is the most scientific religion.
Buddhists wrongly deny a creator.
Everyone knows all things are impermanent.
test.why: The first sentence attributes the teaching to Buddhists without judging or ranking.

test.q: What is one reason the 1893 World's Parliament of Religions in Chicago is remembered?
choices: It created the New Testament canon
It brought speakers such as Vivekananda and Dharmapala to American audiences
It translated the Qur'an into English
It ended all religious disagreement
test.why: The Parliament introduced many Americans to teachers such as Vivekananda and Dharmapala, though its pluralism was uneven.

write.prompt: Do translation and interpretation change what a sacred text means? Answer using two or three texts from this unit, such as Exodus 20:13, Isaiah 7:14, the Song of Songs or the Qur'an's view of translation. Explain how each community reads its text and why.
tips: Name the text and the translation for every passage you quote.
Attribute every belief to its tradition or group, such as many Protestants or Muslims believe.
Compare how communities read the same text rather than judging which reading is right.
Use the unit's terms, such as interpretation, context, allegory and canon, and explain them.
Show diversity inside a tradition where it matters, not only between traditions.
